phonemes.desc: The root bělъ, 'white, shining' — an Indo-European word for light (compare Lithuanian balta, Sanskrit bhāla-).
The linking syllable of the compound, short and open.
bogъ, 'god, share, portion' — the common Slavic word for deity.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BYEH-loh-bohg' — literally 'White God,' the exact mirror of Chernobog, 'Black God.'

kin.label: His opposite

kin.label: Indo-European

pronunciation.note: Belobog is single-tier Tier 2: the name is a transparent compound — bělъ 'white' + bogъ 'god' — and ASCII loses nothing. His existence as a worshiped god is attested only once (Cosmas), which is less than his modern fame assumes; the restoration preserves the name, not a proven cult.

domains.title: Belobog
domains.subtitle: Light
domains.lead: Belobog — the White God of the Slavs, lord of light, good, and fortune — is known from a single medieval chronicle line and a wide scatter of folklore. He is the bright half of the famous Slavic dualism: the good god who stands opposite the Black God of evil.

cards.name: The White God
cards.desc: His very name is his office: bělъ, 'white' — light, brightness, and the good they signify.

cards.name: Good Fortune
cards.desc: In folklore his name attached to the household's luck — the kept wreath and grain that carried prosperity.

cards.name: Counter of the Black God
cards.desc: He exists in structure as much as in story — the bright pole balancing Chernobog's darkness.

cards.name: The Chronicle God
cards.desc: 'Zeloboch' among the demons of Cosmas of Prague — one line, two words, a whole theology.

symbols.name: White (Bělъ)
symbols.meaning: Light itself — the color-word at the root of his name and of Slavic words for dawn and brightness

symbols.name: The Harvest Wreath
symbols.meaning: The last-sheaf wreath called belobog in Polish and Russian folklore, kept till spring to house the field's fortune

symbols.name: The Waxing Light
symbols.meaning: The growing half of the year — the season attributed, in folk reconstruction, to his governance

symbols.name: The Honored Seat
symbols.meaning: The right-hand place at table and hearth — the 'white' side in Slavic custom, opposite the unclean left

mythology.lead: Belobog has no native mythology in the epic sense — no adventures, no genealogy, no cycle. What he has is an attestation, an opposite, and a folklore. His four 'myths' are therefore documents of how a name can carry an entire cosmology on almost no narrative at all.

myths.title: Zeloboch of the Czech Chronicle
myths.text: The only medieval author to name Belobog is Cosmas of Prague, whose Chronica Boemorum (c. 1125, Book I.4) describes the pre-Christian Czechs sacrificing to demons — and lists among them Zeloboch, the chronicler's Latinized rendering of Belobog, alongside gods of the sky, the harvest, and fortune. The sentence is a sneer from a Christian cleric, and its spelling is garbled; yet it proves that around 1100 a 'White God' received offerings in Bohemia. Cosmas is careful to mock the whole catalogue — sky, harvest, and fortune gods jumbled together — which is exactly why scholars mine his scorn for the only list of Czech deities that survives. No myth accompanies the name.No myth accompanies the name. But the attestation does real work: it converts Belobog from a scholarly inference into a historical god, however thinly witnessed — one line carrying the whole bright half of Slavic dualism.

myths.title: Chernobog at Rethra
myths.text: Belobog's structure is completed by his opposite. Helmold of Bosau (Chronica Slavorum I.52, c. 1172) reports that the Slavs acknowledged a god of all evil 'whom they call the Black One' — Chernobog — and modern scholarship assembles the pair: White God and Black God, light and evil, the Slavic dualism (Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian; Rosik, Białobóg). Later folklore strengthens the pairing: across the Slavic world the year's good and ill fortune are personified as opposed powers, and the White God's wreath is the benign half of that old bookkeeping. Historians rightly cautionHistorians rightly caution that the two attestations come from different peoples, centuries, and authors — no text shows the pair worshiped together. The dualism is thus partly reconstruction. Still, the reconstruction rests on two independent medieval witnesses: wherever the sources reach the Slavic gods, they find darkness named — and naming darkness implies, at least to us, its bright counterpart.

myths.title: Belobog in the Last Sheaf
myths.text: Slavic harvest folklore preserved the god's name as a thing. Across Poland and Russia, the final sheaf of the harvest was shaped into a wreath called belobog ('white god') and kept in the house — above the door, by the icons, or in the granary — until the spring sowing, when its grain went back into the field to carry the year's fortune forward (records collected in nineteenth-century ethnography; discussed by Gieysztor and Rosik). Ethnographers found the wreath hung beside the household icons — a quiet index of how long a pagan guest can lodge in a Christian home without ever being named aloud. The custom binds the White GodThe custom binds the White God to the oldest agricultural contract: prosperity is a guest that must be housed, fed, and returned. Whatever his theology, Belobog lived in the rafters of Slavic farmhouses within living memory of the ethnographers.

myths.title: Belobog in the Romantic Mirror
myths.text: After the medieval notices fell silent, Belobog was re-created. Nineteenth-century comparative mythologists, holding the chronicle fragments and the harvest folklore together, rebuilt him as the beneficent pole of a Slavic cosmic dualism — and the Romantic national movements embraced the result: Poland's and Russia's revivals found in the White God a native answer to imported heavens. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries Rodnovery (Slavic neopaganism) went further and returned him to actual worship. The Romantic Belobog was assembled with the tools of the era — comparative grammar, solar mythology, national longing — and the modern scholarship of Gieysztor and Rosik has painstakingly separated the three layers: attestation, folklore, and wish. This modern Belobog is honest only when labeled:This modern Belobog is honest only when labeled: a reconstruction on medieval bones, beloved precisely because it lets a post-Christian people pray in its own oldest vocabulary.

lore.syncretism: Belobog's closest ancient analogue was noticed early: Iranian dualism, with its opposed Spenta Mainyu and Angra Mainyu, offers the famous parallel, and comparative works (Gieysztor; Eliade's surveys of Balkan and Slavic religion) discuss whether Slavic dualism is inherited Indo-European structure, Iranian contact in the Carpathian centuries, or Christian devil-cult projected backward. The honest answer is that the evidence cannot decide. Christianization certainly re-mapped the pair: Chernobog slid toward the Christian devil, while Belobog's light-office was absorbed by Christ — the harvest wreath survived longest precisely where it could pose as a Christian household charm. In the reverse direction, modern Rodnovery has reabsorbed Christian folk practice into the White God's cult. Belobog is thus a palimpsest: pagan name, Christian overlay, pagan revival — each layer legible.
lore.culturalLegacy: Belobog's name lives wherever Slavic says 'white': in Bělehrad — Belgrade, 'the White City' — and in a family of names and words built on the same root. His cultural afterlife, though, belongs to the modern era. He is the emblem of Slavic pre-Christian heritage in schoolbooks, in Romantic poetry, and increasingly in popular culture — fantasy fiction and games have discovered the White God alongside Chernobog, exporting the pair to a global audience that rarely suspects how thin the medieval evidence is. For Slavic neopagans he is an actively worshiped deity of light and prosperity. The folklore core — the kept wreath, the honored right-hand seat, the luck of the household — persists in attenuated custom. A god of one chronicle line thus presides over a modern renaissance, his name a standing reminder that a civilization's bright self-image needs only a few words to survive.
lore.extendedMeditation: Belobog is a study in the birth of a god from a grammar of opposites. Nobody told a story about him — no wooing, no war, no journey — and yet the name alone did the work that myths do elsewhere: it told the Slavs what kind of universe they lived in, one with a bright side and a dark side and a word for each. There is a deep logic in deriving the god of good from the adjective 'white': goodness as visibility, cleanliness, daylight — the things a farming people could literally see. His Black counterpart completes the lesson: evil as the dark, the unclean, the left hand. Modern readers should hold the reconstruction lightly and the intuition firmly. The intuition — that fortune is a presence to be housed and fed, that light deserves a name of its own — is older than any chronicle, and it is what the White God genuinely guards.
lore.archaeology: There is no archaeology of Belobog: no image, temple, or inscription bearing his name has been found, and no Slavic sanctuary excavated to date can be assigned to him. The great Slavic cult sites belong to other gods — Arkona's temple of Svetovid on Rügen (destroyed 1168, described by Saxo Grammaticus), the debated 'Rethra' of Helmold's Black God — and the famous carved idols (the Zbruch pillar) name no deity at all. Belobog's evidence is documentary (Cosmas, Helmold) and ethnographic (the harvest-wreath records). The absence is not trivial: it means the White God belongs to that large class of ancient deities known only through the words of their adversaries — a god whose temples were wooden, seasonal, and gone.
